title: Squid axons, voltage clamp, and the experiments of Hodgkin and Huxley
text:
CHAPTER 5. THE ACTION POTENTIAL
SECTION 5.1. SQUID AXONS, VOLTAGE CLAMP, AND THE EXPERIMENTS OF HODGKIN AND HUXLEY

The problem in 1930

By about 1930, the basic facts about nerve impulses were known. Impulses are electrical. They travel along nerve fibers at speeds from about a meter per second to tens of meters per second. They are all-or-none: a stimulus below threshold produces no impulse, while any stimulus above threshold produces an impulse of the same size. After an impulse, there is a brief refractory period during which the fiber cannot fire again, or can fire only with a stronger stimulus. Bernstein's membrane hypothesis suggested that the resting potential is due to potassium permeability and that the impulse involves a breakdown of the membrane's selectivity.

But no one had recorded the voltage across the membrane of a single nerve fiber directly, from inside, because nerve fibers are thin, mostly a few micrometers or less in diameter. All recordings were made from outside, which gives a distorted, attenuated signal. And no one knew which ions moved, when, or why. The answer came from an unlikely animal: the squid.

The squid giant axon

In 1936, the British zoologist John Zachary Young, working on the anatomy of cephalopods, drew attention to the giant nerve fibers in the squid. Squid have a jet propulsion escape system: when threatened, they contract the muscles of the mantle rapidly, squirting water out to shoot backward. The nerve fibers that trigger this contraction need to conduct very fast, and one way to increase conduction speed in an unmyelinated fiber is to make it thicker. (We will see why in section 5.3 on cable theory.) Squid giant axons can be up to about half a millimeter in diameter, and sometimes more, roughly 100 times thicker than a typical mammalian axon. Young realized that these structures, which some earlier workers had thought were blood vessels, were actually single nerve fibers.

A fiber half a millimeter across is large enough to insert a wire electrode inside, along its length. This changed everything. For an engineer, this is a familiar strategy: if a component is too small to measure, find a scaled-up version of the same system.

Hodgkin and Huxley

Alan Lloyd Hodgkin (1914 to 1998) and Andrew Fielding Huxley (1917 to 2012) were both at Cambridge University. Hodgkin had already done important work on nerve conduction in crab axons, showing that local circuit currents spread ahead of the impulse. Huxley was a student with strong skills in physics, mathematics, and instrument building. In 1939, at the Marine Biological Association laboratory in Plymouth, England, where squid were available, they inserted a fine electrode longitudinally into a squid giant axon and recorded the membrane potential directly from inside.

Their result, published as a short note in Nature in 1939, showed something surprising. The resting potential was about -45 to -50 mV (inside negative), consistent with expectations. But during the action potential, the membrane potential did not simply collapse to zero, as Bernstein's hypothesis predicted. It overshot zero and became positive inside, by tens of millivolts. Kenneth Cole and Howard Curtis, working in the United States at Woods Hole, obtained similar results with squid axons at about the same time.

Then the Second World War interrupted the research. Both Hodgkin and Huxley worked on military projects, Hodgkin on airborne radar and Huxley on operational research for anti-aircraft gunnery. This work deepened their experience with electronics and feedback systems, which would prove valuable.

The sodium hypothesis

After the war, Hodgkin and Bernard Katz tested the idea that the overshoot is caused by a selective increase in sodium permeability. If the membrane during the action potential becomes highly permeable to sodium, then its potential should approach the sodium equilibrium potential E_Na, which is positive. In 1949, Hodgkin and Katz showed that reducing the sodium concentration in the bathing solution reduced the overshoot, roughly as predicted by the Nernst and GHK equations (section 2.3). Replacing sodium with an impermeant substitute (choline, for example) could abolish the action potential. This was strong evidence for the sodium hypothesis.

But to understand the mechanism fully, they needed to know how the permeabilities to sodium and potassium change over time and with voltage. That was difficult because in a normal action potential, everything changes at once: the voltage changes, which changes the permeabilities, which changes the currents, which change the voltage. It is a feedback loop. To study it, they needed to break the loop.

The voltage clamp

The voltage clamp is an electronic feedback system that holds the membrane potential at a chosen value, regardless of what currents the membrane produces. The concept was developed by Kenneth Cole and George Marmont in the late 1940s at Woods Hole, and Hodgkin, Huxley, and Katz developed their own version and used it systematically.

Here is how it works. Two wires are inserted inside the axon: one to measure the voltage, and one to inject current. The measured membrane voltage is compared to a desired "command" voltage by a high-gain amplifier. If the membrane voltage differs from the command, the amplifier injects current to correct it. Because the gain is high, the error is kept very small, and the membrane is effectively "clamped" at the command voltage. The current that the amplifier must inject to hold the voltage constant is equal and opposite to the current flowing through the membrane's ion channels (after a brief capacitive transient). So by measuring the injected current, you measure the membrane current at a fixed voltage.

For a mechatronics student, this is a familiar negative feedback control loop: a setpoint (command voltage), a sensor (voltage electrode), a controller (high-gain amplifier), and an actuator (current electrode). The membrane's ion channels are a disturbance. The control effort (the injected current) is the measurement of interest. The voltage clamp turns a nonlinear dynamical system into one where you can control one variable (voltage) and measure the response (current) at each value.

Why is clamping voltage so useful? Because the ion channels' behavior depends on voltage. If voltage is held constant, the conductances evolve over time according to their own kinetics at that voltage, without feedback from changing voltage. By stepping the voltage to different values and recording the current over time, one can map out how the conductances depend on voltage and time.

In addition, the long axial wire made the inside of the axon isopotential along its length (a "space clamp"), so that the whole length of membrane under study was at the same voltage, and no propagating impulse could occur.

What the voltage clamp showed

When Hodgkin and Huxley stepped the membrane from rest to a depolarized voltage, they saw a characteristic current pattern:

1. A brief capacitive current spike as the membrane capacitance charged to the new voltage.
2. An early inward current (positive charge flowing into the cell), which rose to a peak within about a millisecond and then declined.
3. A later outward current (positive charge flowing out), which rose more slowly, over a few milliseconds, and was maintained as long as the depolarization lasted.

To determine which ions carried which current, they replaced most of the external sodium with choline. The early inward current disappeared or reversed, while the late outward current was little affected. So the early inward current was carried by sodium, flowing in down its electrochemical gradient. The late outward current was carried by potassium, flowing out. (Later, pharmacological tools made this separation easier: tetrodotoxin, a toxin from pufferfish, blocks the sodium channels, and tetraethylammonium blocks many potassium channels.)

By separating the two currents and dividing each by its driving force (V - E_ion), they calculated the sodium and potassium conductances as functions of voltage and time. They found:

- The sodium conductance increases rapidly upon depolarization (activation) and then, even if depolarization is maintained, decreases again (inactivation). Inactivation takes a few milliseconds. After inactivation, the sodium conductance cannot be reactivated until the membrane is repolarized for a while (recovery from inactivation).
- The potassium conductance increases more slowly upon depolarization, with a delay, and does not inactivate (on the time scale of their experiments). It decreases when the membrane is repolarized.
- Both conductances depend steeply on voltage: larger depolarizations open more channels, faster.

They also showed that when the membrane was suddenly repolarized after a depolarizing step, the conductances did not jump back; they declined smoothly over time. This "tail current" behavior was important for determining the kinetics.

The five papers of 1952

Hodgkin and Huxley, partly with Katz, published their results in a series of five papers in the Journal of Physiology in 1952. The first four described the experiments. The fifth, "A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve," presented a mathematical model that described the conductances with a set of differential equations and showed that the model could reproduce the action potential.

That fifth paper is one of the most important papers in the history of biology. It is also a pioneering example of computational modeling. Hodgkin and Huxley solved the differential equations numerically to compute the shape of the propagated action potential and its speed. Huxley did these calculations largely with a hand-operated mechanical calculator (a Brunsviga), because the Cambridge electronic computer of the time was unavailable to them. The calculations reportedly took weeks. The calculated action potential matched the measured one closely, and the calculated conduction velocity for their conditions was about 18.8 meters per second, close to the experimentally observed value of about 21.2 meters per second.

Hodgkin, Huxley, and John Eccles shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

The mechanism, in words

Putting it all together, the action potential works like this:

1. At rest, potassium conductance is modest, sodium conductance is very small, and the membrane sits near -65 mV (in the modern convention), between E_K and E_Na but closer to E_K.
2. A stimulus depolarizes the membrane slightly. This opens a few sodium channels. Sodium flows in, depolarizing the membrane further. This opens more sodium channels. This is positive feedback.
3. If the depolarization is large enough (threshold), the positive feedback becomes explosive: sodium conductance increases dramatically, and the membrane potential shoots up toward E_Na, about +50 mV. This is the rising phase of the action potential.
4. But two slower processes act as negative feedback. Sodium channels inactivate, so sodium conductance falls. And potassium channels open, so potassium flows out. Both drive the membrane back down.
5. The membrane repolarizes and, because potassium conductance is still elevated, overshoots below the resting potential, toward E_K (the afterhyperpolarization, or undershoot).
6. Potassium channels close slowly, sodium channels recover from inactivation, and the membrane returns to rest.
7. During the period when sodium channels are inactivated, a new action potential cannot be triggered (absolute refractory period). As they recover, a stronger-than-usual stimulus can trigger one (relative refractory period).

This explains the all-or-none property (it is the threshold of a positive feedback loop), the refractory period (sodium inactivation and residual potassium conductance), and the overshoot (approach to E_Na). The whole event lasts about a millisecond or a few milliseconds depending on the cell and temperature.

Importantly, the number of ions that cross the membrane during one action potential is tiny compared with the total number in the axon, especially a large axon. A squid giant axon can fire many thousands of action potentials even with its sodium pump blocked before the concentration gradients run down appreciably. The pump is a slow battery charger; the action potential is a fast discharge of a small fraction of the stored energy.

Gates and channels: a prediction

Hodgkin and Huxley described the conductances with "gating variables," which they imagined as representing the positions of charged particles in the membrane that move in response to voltage and control permeability. They did not know what molecules were involved. But their model contained a prediction: if gating is controlled by charged particles that move in the electric field, then their movement should produce a small current of its own, a "gating current," separate from the ionic current. Gating currents were first measured in the early 1970s, by Clay Armstrong and Francisco Bezanilla and by others. And their idea that the membrane contains discrete paths for ions anticipated the discovery of ion channel proteins. We will follow this story in section 5.4.

Bridge to AI: feedback, positive and negative

The action potential is a beautiful example of a system built from positive and negative feedback loops operating on different time scales. Fast positive feedback (sodium activation) creates an explosive, all-or-none event. Slower negative feedback (sodium inactivation and potassium activation) terminates it and resets the system. This structure, fast excitation followed by slow recovery, appears in many systems: in relaxation oscillators in electronics, in the firing of neurons, in the spread of wildfires and epidemics, and in the dynamics of some economic systems.

In artificial neural networks, there is usually no such dynamic: a standard unit computes its output instantaneously from its inputs. But several lines of AI research use richer dynamics. Spiking neural networks use simplified neuron models that have a threshold, a reset, and sometimes a refractory period and adaptation (a slow negative feedback). Recurrent networks with gating, such as LSTMs and GRUs, use multiplicative gates that open and close depending on inputs, and the gate variables in an LSTM (input, forget, and output gates, which are sigmoid functions between 0 and 1) bear a loose but real resemblance to the gating variables of the Hodgkin-Huxley model, which also range between 0 and 1 and multiply a conductance. The analogy is not exact: LSTM gates are learned functions of the input, while HH gates are voltage-dependent physical processes. But the core idea is shared: a multiplicative variable between 0 and 1 controls the flow of something (ions in one case, information in the other).

The voltage clamp also has an AI analog. By clamping one variable and measuring how the system responds, Hodgkin and Huxley isolated the components of a complex feedback system. In interpretability research on neural networks, researchers do something similar when they fix the activations of some units (clamping) and observe how the rest of the network responds. In both cases, breaking a feedback loop is the key to understanding it.

Summary

- J. Z. Young identified the squid giant axon in 1936; its large diameter allowed electrodes to be inserted inside.
- In 1939 Hodgkin and Huxley (and Cole and Curtis) recorded intracellularly and found that the action potential overshoots zero, contradicting Bernstein's hypothesis.
- Hodgkin and Katz (1949) showed the overshoot depends on external sodium.
- The voltage clamp, a negative feedback circuit developed by Cole and Marmont and used by Hodgkin, Huxley, and Katz, holds the membrane potential constant so that ionic currents can be measured.
- Voltage clamp experiments revealed a fast, inactivating sodium conductance and a slower, non-inactivating potassium conductance, both voltage-dependent.
- Hodgkin and Huxley's 1952 model reproduced the action potential and its conduction velocity; they shared the 1963 Nobel Prize with Eccles.
